extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) evaluating pre-AIA public use and on-sale issues
extracted.subtask_description: Assess whether pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) bars (public use or on-sale) apply to an invention by analyzing facts such as confidentiality, control, offers for sale, readiness for patenting, experimental use, and geographic locus of activities. Apply Pfaff's two-prong test and related Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or Absence of a Confidentiality Agreement is Not Dispositive of the Public Use Issue
rubrics_metrics.description: “The presence or absence of a confidentiality agreement is not dispositive of the public use issue, but ‘is one factor to be considered in assessing all the evidence.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze evidence of public use in the context of policies underlying the public use and on-sale bars (discouraging removal from public domain, prohibiting extension of exploitation period, favoring prompt disclosure). Consider nature of activity, public access/knowledge, and whether confidentiality obligations were imposed (Bernhardt example: restricted exhibition with checked attendee list and escorts led court to remand for totality analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor Allows Another To Use the Invention Without Restriction or Obligation of Secrecy = Public Use
rubrics_metrics.description: “Public use of a claimed invention under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) occurs when the inventor allows another person to use the invention without limitation, restriction or obligation of secrecy to the inventor.” (In re Smith)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence/absence of confidentiality agreement is one factor; must consider time, place, and circumstances showing amount of control inventor retained. Example: sale of seeds to growers and lack of confidentiality rose to public use/on-sale; hidden use without secrecy obligations may be public (Egbert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by Independent Third Parties is Public Use if it 'Informs' the Public or Makes Invention Ascertainable
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsecret use by persons unconnected to inventor or secret use that is ascertainable by inspection/analysis of products sold or publicly displayed may be a 'public use'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If details of inventive machine/process are ascertainable from sold/displayed product, the third party's use is public (Gillman, Dunlop). If third party kept invention as trade secret and details are not ascertainable, then use is not public (W.L. Gore). A device may be prior art if it places claimed features in public's possession even if other aspects remained confidential (Lockwood). Consider factual circumstances and how they comport with policies underlying bars; e.g., allowing many nonconfidential employees access and educating them may 'inform' the public (Chemithon).

rubrics_metrics.name: On-Sale Bar: Definite Sale or Offer More Than One Year Before Filing That Anticipates or Renders Obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: “An impermissible sale has occurred if there was a definite sale, or offer of sale, more than 1 year before the effective filing date of the U.S. application and the subject matter of the sale, or offer to sell, fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered the claimed invention obvious…” (Ferag AG v. Quipp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Pfaff two-prong test: (1) product must be subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily experimental; (2) invention must be ready for patenting. Use traditional contract law (UCC) to determine whether a commercial offer for sale occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: To be 'On Sale' the Product Must Bear Hallmarks of a Commercial Sale (UCC §2-106)
rubrics_metrics.description: “[T]o be ‘on sale’ under § 102(b), a product must be the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale,” and must bear general hallmarks of a sale pursuant to Section 2-106 of the UCC (passage of title as helpful indicator). (Medicines Co. v. Hospira)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage of title suggests inventor gave up interest/control. Transactions where title/right to market do not pass (e.g., contract manufacturer selling services to inventor) may not constitute invalidating sales. Determine who receives title/marketing rights and whether the product was commercially marketed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Sale May Bar a Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: “An invention may be deemed to be ‘on sale’ even though the sale was conditional.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sale conditioned on buyer satisfaction does not automatically show the sale was for experimental purposes; conditional terms alone do not avoid the on-sale bar (Strong v. General Elec.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprofit Sale May Bar a Patent (Profit Not Required)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A ‘sale’ need not be for profit to bar a patent. If the sale was for the commercial exploitation of the invention, it is ‘on sale’ within the meaning of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial exploitation—regardless of whether profit is realized—can trigger the on-sale bar (In re Dybel). Focus on purpose and commercial exploitation rather than profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Single Sale or Offer To Sell May Bar a Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a single sale or offer to sell the invention may bar patentability under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent recognizes that one instance of sale/offer can be sufficient (Consolidated Fruit-Jar; Atlantic Thermoplastics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of Rights/Assignment is Not Per Se a Sale of the Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment or sale of rights in the invention/potential patent rights is not a sale of 'the invention' within the meaning of pre-AIA §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between assignments/licenses that transfer rights (may not per se trigger on-sale) and licenses that operate like immediate transfer of product (which can trigger on-sale). Examples: certain licenses (exclusive marketing rights) may not trigger bar, while software licenses that immediately transfer product may. See Moleculon, Elan, In re Kollar, Group One.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buyer Must Be Uncontrolled by the Seller for Sale to Trigger Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale or offer for sale must take place between separate entities; if parties are related, the statutory bar depends on whether seller controls purchaser so invention remains out of public's hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related-party transactions may avoid a bar if purchaser has independent control; if purchaser is effectively controlled by seller, the sale can be a statutory bar (In re Caveney; Ferag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer for Sale Must Rise to Level of a Commercial Offer (Definite Offer with Material Terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Only an offer which rises to the level of a commercial offer for sale, one which the other party could make into a binding contract by simple acceptance (assuming consideration), constitutes an offer for sale under §102(b).” (Group One v. Hallmark)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material terms (price, quantities, time/place of delivery, product specifications) should be present; communications lacking such terms may not be contractual offers (Elan). An offer to license in future development is not necessarily an offer to sell the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejected or Unreceived Offer for Sale Is Sufficient to Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere offer to sell is sufficient commercial activity to bar a patent; even a rejected or unreceived offer may create an on-sale bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: In re Theis; UMC Elecs.; Wende. The focus is on objective offer activity, not acceptance or receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery Not Required to Trigger On-Sale Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that a sale be consummated for the bar to operate; a signed purchase agreement prior to the critical date can constitute a commercial offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery or exchange of money after the critical date does not negate a prior on-sale bar if the agreement existed before the critical date (Buildex; Weatherchem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller Need Not Have Goods 'On Hand' When Offer is Made
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods need not be on hand and transferred at the time of the sale or offer; the date of the offer for sale is the effective date of the on-sale activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the invention must be complete and 'ready for patenting' before the critical date (Pfaff). If inventor was not close to completion, an offer may not trigger the bar (Micro Chemical). Presence of a makeshift model or samples can support an on-sale finding (Barmag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale Activity Need Not Be Public
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike public use, there is no requirement that 'on sale' activity be 'public.' 'Public' modifies 'use' only, not 'sale.' (Hobbs v. United States)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-sale inquiries focus on whether sale/offer occurred, not on public accessibility of the transaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's Consent to Sale Is Not Required for On-Sale Bar (Third-Party Sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was placed on sale by a third party who obtained the invention from the inventor, a patent is barred even if the inventor did not consent or know of the sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party commercialization of an invention obtained from the inventor can trigger the bar (Electric Storage Battery; CTS Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Evidence Controls: Need Proof That Sold/Offered Product Embodies the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Key question is whether the inventor sold or offered for sale a product that embodies the invention claimed in the application; objective evidence (contracts, descriptions, correspondence, drawings, testimony) controls over uncommunicated intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchaser's reasonable belief as to what was offered is relevant (Envirotech). Objective communications specifying inventive design (order confirmations, contracts) can establish on-sale activity (Ferag; RCA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprior-Art Publications May Serve as Evidence of Prior Sale by Third Parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts identifying a product's vendor with buyer-relevant information (contacts, price, documentation, release/installation dates) before applicant's critical date may provide sufficient evidence of prior sale by a third party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonprior-art publications with release/installation dates have supported examiner rejections under pre-AIA 102(b)/103 (In re Epstein). Use publication dates and vendor identification as objective evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Invention Must Be 'Ready for Patenting' (Pfaff Two-Prong: Offer + Readiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pfaff test: (1) the product must be the subject of a commercial offer for sale; (2) the invention must be ready for patenting (either reduced to practice or described in drawings/other descriptions sufficiently specific to enable POSITA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ready for patenting can be demonstrated by reduction to practice before the critical date or by sufficiently specific drawings/specifications enabling a person skilled in the art. Inventions embodied in products that inherently possess each claimed limitation satisfy 'ready for patenting' even if parties did not know details (Pfaff; Weatherchem; Abbott).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual Reduction to Practice Before Sale Bars Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was actually reduced to practice before being sold or offered for sale more than one year before filing, a patent will be barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice typically requires testing under actual working conditions to demonstrate practical utility, unless invention's simplicity makes operability clear (Vanmoor; Field; Steinberg). Detailed drawings used to produce sold embodiments can establish reduction to practice (Vanmoor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention Need Not Be Ready for Commercial Marketing to Be 'Ready for Patenting'
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention need not be ready for satisfactory commercial marketing for sale to bar a patent; readiness for patenting is a lower threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on technical readiness (enablement/embodiment of claimed limitations) rather than commercial marketability (Atlantic Thermoplastics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits/Declarations Under 37 C.F.R. 1.131 May Constitute Admissions of Prior Completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations submitted under 37 C.F.R. 1.131 to swear behind a reference may constitute, among other things, an admission that an invention was 'complete' more than one year before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such submissions can be used against applicant as admissions (In re Foster; Dart Indus.). See MPEP § 715.10 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a Process: Know-How Sale vs Sale of Product Made by Process
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed process (series of acts/steps) is not sold in same sense as a tangible product; sale of 'know-how' may not be a 'sale' of the invention, but sale of a product made by the claimed process by patentee or licensee can constitute a sale of the process under pre-AIA §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sale of a product embodying the process or offering to perform the process can trigger the on-sale bar for process claims (In re Kollar; D.L. Auld; W.L. Gore). Sale of a prior-art device that only later is used to practice the method may not trigger the bar if it was not used to practice the method before the critical date (Poly-America).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Requirement: 'In This Country' (US) for Pre-AIA 102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), public use or on-sale activity must take place in the United States, though substantial prefatory activity in the U.S. or offers originating in the U.S. may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacture and delivery occurring in a foreign country generally do not trigger the on-sale bar (Gandy), but U.S.-originating offers or substantial U.S. prefatory activity (offers communicated to purchasers in U.S.) can bring foreign transactions within the statute (Robbins; CTS Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Use Doctrine: Primary Purpose Must Be Experimentation, Not Commercial Exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental use doctrine asks whether the primary purpose of the inventor at time of sale was to conduct experimentation; experimentation must be the primary purpose and commercial exploitation only incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental use is a bona fide effort to perfect the invention or ascertain whether it will answer its intended purpose. Market testing to gauge consumer demand is commercial, not experimental, and does not qualify (Allen Eng'g; LaBounty; In re Smith; EZ Dock). Burden of proof on applicant is high where commercial exploitation is evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Exploitation Must Legitimately Advance Development Towards Completion to Qualify as Experimental
rubrics_metrics.description: As degree of commercial exploitation increases, the burden on applicant to establish clear and convincing evidence of experimental activity increases; commercial activity that does not legitimately advance development is not experimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner finds prima facie sale/offer, applicant will rarely meet burden unless clear and convincing evidence of necessity of experimentation is shown. There can be circumstances permitting experimentation in a commercial atmosphere, but necessity and bona fides must be demonstrated.
